metadata.title: How perceived teaching autonomy predicts job satisfaction in China: The mediating role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of school climate

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data restricted to Shanghai (the only Chinese city participating in TALIS 2018), with a stratified sample of 3,976 lower-secondary teachers from 198 schools. For estimation, the authors incorporate TALIS teacher final weights (TCHWGT) and 100 BRR replicate weights (TRWGT1–TRWGT100) to account for the complex sampling design. Standard errors are adjusted using BRR within Mplus 8.3, and model parameters are estimated with maximum likelihood (ML). Missing demographic information is handled via listwise deletion, while other missingness is addressed using FIML in Mplus 8.3 (MAR assumption), so the weighting and missing-data procedures are applied within the SEM framework rather than as a separate ML preprocessing step.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for Shanghai (China), with a stratified sample of 3,976 lower-secondary teachers from 198 schools. The analytic sample size reported in Table 1 is N=3,944, indicating exclusions after missing-data handling. Missing demographic information was removed via listwise deletion; remaining missing data were handled using Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) in Mplus 8.3 under a missing-at-random (MAR) assumption.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation model (BRR-weighted ML in Mplus): Total effect of teaching autonomy on job satisfaction β=0.272, t=5.192, p<0.001; Direct effect β=0.209, t=3.669, p<0.001; Indirect effect via self-efficacy β=0.063, t=2.736, p=0.006. Moderation: direct path interaction (Teaching autonomy × School climate → Job satisfaction) β=0.135, t=2.753, p=0.006; model R² (Job satisfaction)=0.244, p<0.001; SRMR=0.049.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged teaching autonomy, teacher self-efficacy, and school climate (with teaching experience as a control) to predict job satisfaction, finding that teaching autonomy had a significant positive direct effect and also an indirect effect through self-efficacy, with the autonomy–satisfaction link amplified by supportive school climate. This indicates that teacher autonomy policies should be paired with school-climate improvements to translate autonomy into higher teacher well-being, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for Shanghai (China), focusing on lower-secondary teachers (analytic N=3,944; 198 schools). Using BRR-weighted maximum likelihood estimation in Mplus 8.3, the authors test a triple moderated mediation model where teaching autonomy predicts job satisfaction directly and indirectly via teacher self-efficacy, while school climate moderates the direct and mediated pathways. Teaching autonomy shows a significant total effect on job satisfaction (β=0.272, t=5.192, p<0.001) with partial mediation by self-efficacy (indirect effect β=0.063, t=2.736, p=0.006) and a significant direct effect (β=0.209, t=3.669, p<0.001). School climate significantly moderates all pathways, including the direct interaction (β=0.135, t=2.753, p=0.006), and the model explains 24.4% of variance in job satisfaction (R²=0.244). Limitations include reliance on self-reports, cross-sectional data (no causal inference), and the need for multilevel modeling to better address school-level clustering.
